what_its_for: Anifrolumab-fnia is used to treat moderate to severe systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), also known as lupus, in adults who are already taking other lupus medicines. Lupus is a disease where your immune system mistakenly attacks your own body. This medicine helps calm down that overactive immune response to reduce lupus symptoms like joint pain, skin rashes, and fatigue.
how_to_take: This medicine is given as an intravenous (IV) infusion, meaning it is injected slowly into a vein through an IV line. A healthcare provider will give you this infusion in a clinic or infusion center. Each infusion takes about 30 minutes. You will be watched by healthcare staff during and for a short time after your infusion to make sure you do not have a reaction.
dosing: The usual adult dose is 300 mg given once every 4 weeks (about once a month) as an IV infusion. Your doctor will decide the right dose and schedule for you. Always follow your doctor's instructions exactly and do not try to adjust your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss your scheduled infusion appointment, contact your doctor or infusion center as soon as possible to reschedule. Try to get back on your regular 4-week schedule. Do not double up on doses to make up for a missed one.
storage: This medicine is stored and prepared by healthcare professionals at the clinic or infusion center. You do not need to store it at home. If you have questions about how the medicine is handled, ask your healthcare provider.
what_to_avoid: Avoid getting live vaccines while taking this medicine, as it weakens your immune system and live vaccines could cause infection. Talk to your doctor before getting any vaccinations. Try to avoid close contact with people who are sick, and practice good handwashing to lower your risk of infections. Let your doctor know right away if you develop signs of infection such as fever, chills, cough, or sore throat.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: signs of a serious allergic or infusion reaction (such as trouble breathing, chest tightness, severe rash, swelling of the face or throat, dizziness, or fast heartbeat); signs of infection (fever, chills, body aches, cough, painful urination); unusual tiredness or weakness; shingles or cold sore outbreak; or any new or worsening symptoms. Also tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding.
when_it_works: Anifrolumab-fnia does not work right away. It may take several weeks to a few months before you notice an improvement in your lupus symptoms. It is important to keep all of your scheduled infusion appointments and continue taking your other lupus medicines unless your doctor tells you otherwise. Do not stop treatment without talking to your doctor first.
special_populations: Pregnant or breastfeeding women: This medicine may harm an unborn baby. Use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 12 weeks after your last dose. Talk to your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Elderly patients: No special dose adjustment is needed, but your doctor will monitor you closely. Children: This medicine is not approved for use in patients under 18 years of age. Patients with infections: Tell your doctor about any active infections before starting this medicine, as it can increase your risk of getting infections.
